papers.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

papers.title: Atheism and Cross-Country National Cognitive Skills: Evidence from a Beta Regression Analysis
papers.abstract: This study performs a beta regression analysis to investigate how country-level cognitive skills---measured using harmonized large-scale international educational assessments and expressed on an IQ-type scale---are associated with the prevalence of atheism in 131 countries. We find that this association is nonlinear: at low levels of cognitive skills, increases are associated with lower expected levels of atheism, whereas beyond a threshold, they are associated with higher expected atheism rates. This turning point is estimated to occur at approximately 65 on the IQ-type scale. The strength and location of the relationship vary across regions. We estimate elasticities of expected atheism rates with respect to cognitive skills for all countries in the sample and introduce the concept of the atheism gap to identify countries where observed prevalence is substantially higher or lower than predicted by their conditioning variables.

papers.title: PrO Filtering via Kernel Mean Embedding Dynamics
papers.abstract: Filtering methods are routinely deployed with misspecified state-space models, where Bayesian filters can diverge and become overconfident. Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering is a recent, hyperparameter-free alternative that was demonstrated to outperform (generalised) Bayesian filtering methods when either the dynamical model or the measurement model is structurally misspecified. This can be attributed to \emph{hedging} behaviour: when an observation conflicts with the forecast, the PrO update places mass near both. Yet existing implementations of PrO filtering rely on unimodal (Gaussian) approximations, whose ability to effectively hedge is limited. This paper develops the first nonparametric, particle-based implementation of PrO filtering. The key obstacle, that PrO filtering distributions are only implicitly defined, is overcome by constructing a path from the predictive to the PrO filtering distribution whose rate is available in closed form, enabling the use of kernel mean embedding dynamics for measure transport. The resulting algorithm requires only simulation from the dynamical model and evaluations of the likelihood, with neither importance weights nor the predictive density. Moreover, as we prove, the number of pseudo-time steps it requires does not grow with the outlyingness of the observation, in contrast to transport along the Bayesian tempering path. An empirical assessment shows substantial improvement over Gaussian variation of PrO filtering in challenging nonlinear examples where Gaussian approximation is unreasonably limited.

papers.title: Resolving cell states in spatial transcriptomics with SCATTER
papers.abstract: A capture spot can contain transcripts from multiple cell types. Differences between spots may reflect changes in cell-type proportions, expression within a cell type, or both, making local cell-type expression difficult to infer from mixed counts. We developed SCATTER to estimate cell-type proportions and relative expression profiles for each cell type at each spot from spatial transcriptomic counts, coordinates, and annotated single-cell reference data. SCATTER weights reference cell profiles using local spatial context, then jointly fits the resulting profiles and cell-type proportions to reconstruct spot counts. Cell2location estimates regularize the proportions. After fitting, SCATTER uses learned gene-specific calibration factors and fitted proportions to allocate observed counts among cell types. In five pseudo-spot benchmarks constructed from imaging data, SCATTER achieved higher cross-spot correlations with measured expression for 82.8-99.8% of evaluated gene-cell type pairs in pairwise comparisons with DestVI, PANDA, and STged. In breast cancer Xenium data, it recovered gene expression associated with the tumor neighborhood and regulon scores. In breast cancer Visium data, inferred stromal and macrophage expression showed distinct associations with neighborhood malignant cell proportions. In multiple sclerosis brain tissue, SCATTER recovered lesion-associated glial expression programs. In colorectal cancer Visium HD data, it mapped cell-type-specific programs at the invasive front and ranked candidate ligand-receptor pairs. SCATTER enables analysis of spatial expression variation within cell types from mixed tissue measurements.

papers.title: Modeling time series of high-resolution spectra using the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition with application to radial velocity exoplanet searches
papers.abstract: We describe a framework for building low-rank separable expansions to model spectroscopic data from systems with time-varying spectra, in settings where the spectral dimension is finely sampled (in wavelength), but the temporal dimension is sparsely and possibly irregulary sampled. The motivating application is detection and characterization of small exoplanets, e.g., Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. Such planets cannot be seen directly, but can be detected via the minute Doppler shifts of the host star spectrum due to the star's motion as the planet and star revolve around their mutual center of mass. Current instruments are reaching the precision necessary to detect the ~10 cm/s motions corresponding to an exo-Earth. But the small Doppler shifts from such low-amplitude orbital motion can be masked or mimicked by the effects of stellar activity on the surface of the host star. e.g., starspots (dark regions), faculae (bright filaments), etc. One technique astronomers have used to try to model the stellar activity component of the signal is PCA, applied to an ensemble of spectra collected over time. But PCA neglects the continuous function nature of a spectrum at a given time, and the continuous evolution of spectra over time. We address model building from a function approximation perspective, via the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition (HSD). This provides a PCA-like low-rank decomposition of a dynamic spectrum, but it explicitly accounts for time dependence, both estimating temporal basis functions, and accounting for irregular temporal sampling when estimating spectral basis functions. We show that HSD improves the fidelity of a fixed-order model of the dynamic spectrum of a Sun-like star with a starspot, with mean squared error for spectral basis functions many times smaller than achieved via PCA when spectra are randomly sampled sparsely and irregularly in time.

papers.title: ENSO-linked redistribution of post-monsoon tropical cyclone energy between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal: 1982--2025
papers.abstract: Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean (NIO) form in two sub-basins, the Arabian Sea (AS) and the Bay of Bengal (BoB), which are usually studied separately, with their relationship to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) treated as stationary. We develop a joint inter-basin statistical framework and apply it to 416 disturbances from quality-controlled IBTrACS best tracks for 1982--2025, with harmonised IMD and JTWC intensities, ERA5 and ERSSTv5. The framework tests whether ENSO changes the basin total or redistributes energy between the sub-basins, separates its effect on formation from that on intensification, attributes each sub-basin's response to environmental terms along individual tracks, and tests stationarity and the record length needed to detect trends. In October-December, ENSO redistributes rather than changes the total: for a one-standard-deviation increase in Niño-3.4 (about 1 $^\circ$C), accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) is multiplied by 1.89 in the AS and by 0.63 in the BoB, while the NIO total shows no detectable change (factor 0.99 [0.74, 1.32]). ENSO acts on intensification, with no detectable effect on formation: the odds that a cyclonic storm becomes very severe rise about fourfold in the AS and halve in the BoB, through lower vertical wind shear (VWS) over the AS and weaker low-level vorticity over the BoB. The relationship has changed: El Niño lowered total NIO energy in 1982--2003, but in 2004-2025 AS gains balanced BoB losses (change p = 0.016). Very severe storms and rapid intensification increased in the AS only, and no 15-year window detects this increase, so about three decades of data are needed. The post-monsoon IOD signal can hardly be separated from ENSO, and August Niño-3.4 gives modest skill for the AS-BoB partition but none for the basin total.

papers.title: Who Fills the Gap? Role Similarity and Teammates' Minutes When NBA Players Are Ruled Out
papers.abstract: When a core player is ruled out before an NBA game, do teammates whose statistical role resembles that of the removed set (every rotation player ruled out, about three per case) play more? Using injury reports stamped at least six hours before tip-off and rosters reconstructed after the season, we study 2,441 team-games from 2023-24 to 2025-26 in which a core player was ruled out for a medical reason. Among teammates in the same game, one within-case standard deviation more similarity in role profile (three-point attempts, assists and rebounds per minute) goes with about 0.63 more minutes, holding reference minutes and headroom fixed (p < 0.0001); this compares teammates within a game, not the minutes gained because of the absence. The pattern holds in two earlier seasons and in exploratory within-player and without-and-with comparisons. Whether similarity adds to listed position is not settled. The association is small and yielded no statistically detectable reduction in the error of the retrospective minute forecasts we tested. Role coverage, how much of the missing minutes and roles the remaining rotation could restore, showed no consistent incremental association with team role output or the final margin.

papers.title: The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model as a Statistical Model: Identification, Estimation, and Model Comparison
papers.abstract: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) distinguishes stable differences between people from lagged associations within individuals. We use a matrix representation to study its statistical properties for p variables measured across T waves. We derive a necessary and sufficient rank condition for global identification when transition matrices and innovation covariances vary by wave. Under time-invariant transitions, the condition specifies when three waves suffice. For complete Gaussian trajectories, matrix differentiation yields the profile likelihood score for each covariance and transition block. We also derive the population parameters of the conventional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) when an RI-CLPM with fixed parameters generates the data. Our formulas quantify how CLPM slopes for observed variables differ from RI-CLPM slopes for within-person deviations at each transition. When the RI-CLPM transition matrix is time-invariant, the comparison also covers CLPM slopes pooled across waves. The formulas recover earlier bivariate results and show when cross-lagged slopes can appear, cancel, reverse sign, or change their ordering across models.

papers.title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit
papers.abstract: Preclinical animal studies often allow multiple valid statistical analysis strategies, which can result in different sample sizes required to achieve a target power. Because reducing animal use is an ethical, financial, and practical priority, researchers have a clear incentive to choose the strategy requiring the fewest animals. This may, however, favour an overly optimistic estimate of the sample size required, particularly when prior information is uncertain or biased. This study investigates how minimising sample size across analysis strategies affects statistical power and animal use. We conceptualise this practice as sample size hacking, describe its underlying mechanism, and evaluate its consequences using a simulation study based on a real preclinical cancer study. We varied effect sizes, the level of uncertainty in prior information, and the degree of follow-up bias to assess the resulting sample size reductions and achieved statistical power. Sample size minimisation across analysis strategies substantially reduced the achieved statistical power in several scenarios, particularly for moderate effect sizes and greater uncertainty in prior information. For larger effect sizes or in the presence of follow-up bias, the impact on power was less pronounced, but the resulting reduction in sample size was also smaller. Selecting an analysis strategy solely because it yields the smallest calculated sample size may in fact compromise statistical power, while offering only limited animal savings in other settings. These findings underscore the importance of justifying and pre-specifying the analysis strategy before sample size planning to limit potentially problematic analytical flexibility, reduce the risk of underpowered studies, and promote transparency in preclinical research.

papers.title: The Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model: A Semi-mechanistic Generative Model for Temporal Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Many complex networks involve time-varying relations between more than two nodes. Such networks are naturally modeled by temporal hypergraphs. We propose the Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model (HHCM), a semi-mechanistic model for temporal hypergraphs that combines a Hawkes process to model the timestamps of hyperedges with a noisy copy mechanism to model the nodes present in hyperedges. Each hyperedge is either generated as an exogenous event with a baseline rate or an endogenous event as a noisy copy of a previous hyperedge. Our proposed model can be used for credit attribution, where the objective is to quantify the influence or contribution of a prior hyperedge to a current one. We apply the HHCM to perform attribution on several real network datasets with higher-order relations, including email networks and militarized interstate dispute networks.

papers.title: Projection of multidimensional count data IRT models and their empirical indistinguishability
papers.abstract: Empirical test data is rarely unidimensional. If one dimension is of interest, projective item-response-theory (IRT) models can be used to work with a unidimensional model without neglecting the multidimensionality of the data. This work extends the projective IRT literature to count data IRT models from the Two-Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model framework. We build on the definition of empirical indistinguishability and analytically derive closed-form expressions for discrimination parameters and item intercepts after projection. The dispersion parameters of the projected Two- Parameter Conway-Maxwell-Poisson model are obtained with numerical approximations. The analytical calculations are not limited to the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson distribution. In addition, rotation methods are applied before projection. Results are illustrated and evaluated using empirical data from cognitive ability assessment items and in a simulation study. The projected model performed better in terms of RMSE, Spearman correlation between the true and estimated person parameters, and coverage of 95% confidence intervals based on the Fisher information than an approximation by a standard unidimensional model fitted to multidimensional data. No improvement in bias over the standard unidimensional model, nor improvement across all metrics over the multidimensional model, were observed.

papers.title: Analytical Wald Power for Lagged Coefficients in the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model
papers.abstract: In a longitudinal study, the number of participants and the number of waves both affect how much power the study has to detect a lagged effect. The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) is widely used to study within-person dynamics, but existing approaches to power analysis for this model typically rely on simulation or target likelihood-ratio tests. Starting from the likelihood score, we derive analytical Wald power for each lagged coefficient in the bivariate RI-CLPM. Across 30 designs, we compared our analytical results with power estimates from two R packages, powRICLPM for simulated Wald power and semPower for analytical likelihood-ratio power. The mean absolute difference was less than one percentage point in each comparison. By avoiding repeated simulation and model fitting, the analytical method saves time when evaluating power for a target path across many combinations of sample size (N) and number of waves (T).

papers.title: Stochastic Failure Dynamics in a Model Peptidoglycan Mesh under Hydrolysis and Mechanical Loading
papers.abstract: We develop a minimal stochastic-mechanical model for failure dynamics of the Gram-negative peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall under blocked growth and continued hydrolysis. The cell wall is modelled as a collection of load-bearing cross-sections, with random number of cross-links in each such cross-section, around a fixed degree of cross-linking. To understand failure dynamics of the cell wall under antibacterial agents which prevent insertion of fresh PG material, peptide bonds are progressively excised by hydrolases, while insertion/formation of new bonds is blocked. We compare and contrast rupture dynamics in no-load and load-activated regimes, using extreme value theory and stochastic simulations, deriving limiting laws for system failure in both the long-cell and large crosslinking limits. For a cross-section with many bonds, the mean failure time grows only log- arithmically with bond number, giving diminishing returns from additional cross-linking. In the no-load case, the centered failure time converges to a Gumbel law, though crucially, load changes the centered distribution and accelerates the final stages of collapse. In long cells, failure follows a weakest-link Weibull-type scaling controlled by the least cross-linked regions, with mechanical load reducing the failure-time scale without changing the weakest-link exponent. The fraction of bonds removed before failure tends to zero, showing that collapse can remain highly localized even while the global cross-linking degree stays high. Slowing down growth and other cellular functions is a typical antibiotic escape mechanism for bacteria and in this context, we show that, hydrolase down-regulation uniformly rescales the failure-time distribution and delays collapse, but does not remove the load-induced preference for rupture in weakened regions.

papers.title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis
papers.abstract: In decision-making under uncertainty, additional information can improve decisions but is often costly to acquire. The Value of Information (VoI) quantifies the expected benefit of different information-gathering strategies. The main computational burden in VoI analysis arises from evaluating the expected utility of a strategy over possible outcomes. As each outcome entails solving a computationally expensive optimization problem under uncertainty to determine the optimal decision, efficient estimation of this expectation is crucial. This work focuses on sampling-based estimation and investigates three classical variance-reduction techniques, namely control variates, stratified sampling, and importance sampling, as well as combinations thereof. In particular, we establish a connection between two common VoI formulations through a control variate framework and show how this relationship can be exploited to obtain more efficient VoI estimators. The methodology is assessed using three test cases. The first is an analytical example with a known reference solution, the second involves a fatigue reliability and the third a slope stability application. Our results demonstrate that the relative performance of the sampling methods depends strongly on the problem characteristics. However, suitable combinations of variance-reduction techniques consistently improve efficiency and provide stable VoI estimates across a range of scenarios.

papers.title: Reading the Room with AI: FOMC Deliberation and Growth-at-Risk
papers.abstract: Macro-at-Risk models forecast the growth distribution from public data; policy is set by a committee arguing over their meaning. From FOMC Minutes, public three weeks after each meeting, we add several dimensions of deliberation to a growth quantile model on FRED-MD's 123 series. Only disagreement present in the discussion but absent from the vote lowers out-of-sample loss by 4-6 percent, chiefly in the center, beyond professional, staff and Committee forecasts. Much of deliberation's informational value lies in the recorded discussion itself, and in the disagreement it reveals, rather than in the risk assessments the Committee chooses to state.

papers.title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data
papers.abstract: Knowledge-guided learning methods that incorporate biological graph information into the analysis of structured high-dimensional data, such as genomic data, can improve variable selection and prediction accuracy while yielding more interpretable results. However, these methods typically assume that covariates are measured without error. This assumption is often violated in omics studies involving replicated measurements. To address this gap, we develop the Bayesian Adaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression Solution (BADGERS), a Bayesian framework that jointly accounts for covariate measurement error and incorporates graph information while accommodating varying numbers of replicates across covariates. BADGERS treats the true covariates as latent variables and integrates three key components: a Gaussian errors-in-variables model using replicated measurements to inform the latent true covariates, a Bayesian adaptive graphical lasso with a graph-informed prior to model their dependence structure, and a regression model with an adaptive structured shrinkage prior to leverage graph information and facilitate variable selection. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior sampling. We demonstrate the advantages of BADGERS over existing methods through simulation studies and analyses of gene expression datasets for Alzheimer's disease and multiple myeloma.

papers.title: Guarded Readmission Weighting for Robust Single-Index Frechet Regression
papers.abstract: Single-index Frechet regression reduces the predictor dimension for metric-space responses such as distributions, networks or curves, but its estimators are sensitive to outliers. We propose guarded readmission weighting (GRW), a one-step computation of case weights from the predictors and the response distances, usable with any weighted estimator. GRW starts from a high-breakdown fit to a multidimensional scaling surrogate, readmits cases by an add-one metric Cook's distance, downweights remote predictors and keeps a response isolation factor in the final weights. If fewer than $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of the $n$ cases are replaced, objects far from the uncontaminated responses receive weight zero; under elliptical predictors, weights depending on the predictors only through the index and the Mahalanobis distance keep the population weighted directions in the index subspace. In simulations, three GRW-weighted estimators keep the mean projection distance to the true direction below about 0.5 under up to 30% scattered and 20% clustered bad leverage points, whereas deletion and $α$-distance covariance become much less accurate as contamination grows; $α$-distance covariance is more accurate in most clean, shape-outlier and good-leverage settings. In two applications, under planted contamination, the weighted surrogate-assisted and least squares directions move less than those of methods without GRW.

papers.title: Pseudo-IPD Reconstruction from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves under Unidentified Within-Interval Censoring
papers.abstract: Reconstruction of pseudo-individual patient data (pseudo-IPD) from published Kaplan-Meier curves and number-at-risk tables is widely used to support secondary survival analyses when individual-level data are unavailable. However, the reconstruction is generally not unique because the published information does not determine how censoring is distributed within each risk-table interval. We study the non-identifiability that remains after interval-level event and censoring totals have been reconstructed. Different within-interval censoring placements can yield similarly good Kaplan-Meier agreement but different risk-set and censoring patterns, with possible effects on subsequent analyses. We characterize this non-identifiability, introduce a systematic allocation scheme, and assess its impact on reconstructed pseudo-IPD and downstream analyses. Simulation studies were conducted to examine how within-interval censoring allocation affects pseudo-IPD reconstruction under different risk-table resolutions and censoring settings. The proposed approach was also illustrated using published data from CheckMate 067. Our analysis suggests that considering multiple reconstructions provides a practical way to assess the impact of this non-identifiability on downstream analyses.

papers.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
papers.abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

papers.title: Permutation tests for Poisson network regression: Double semi-partialling, studentized statistics and actor effects
papers.abstract: The multiple regression quadratic assignment procedure (MRQAP) is a standard framework for inference on dyadic network data, and its properties are well established for the linear model. Network outcomes are often counts, modelled by Poisson regression with a log link. We prove that the invariance property of the Frisch--Waugh--Lovell theorem, the only part that double semi-partialling (DSP) requires, survives the nonlinear link. The DSP focal coefficient and its model-based, HC3 and dyadic cluster-robust standard errors coincide with those of the fit on the raw covariates. The choice between relabelling the raw focal array ($X$-permutation) and relabelling its DSP residual acts only on the reference distribution. The test holds its level when the relabelled designs reproduce the dependence that the statistic retains, and DSP reproduces the autocorrelation of the partialled focal covariate. When the raw focal array and its residual share their autocorrelation, the relabelling test holds the nominal level for all three statistics, at covariate correlations up to $0.9$ and in networks of $20$ to $100$ actors. A normal reference rejects a true null at rates up to $0.96$. With sender and receiver effects modelled, every statistic rejects a true null at $0.035$ to $0.070$ in all conditions, and power against a focal effect of $0.10$ rises from at most $32\%$ to at least $99.9\%$. When the actor effects cannot be modelled, adding the sender and receiver means of the nuisance covariates keeps DSP at its level. We give recommendations and illustrate the method on the EIES message-count network.

papers.title: Beyond Gentrification: quantifying the economic, social and cultural dimensions of neighbourhood change through housing markets and digital traces
papers.abstract: Neighbourhood change is a multidimensional process in which economic, demographic, social and cultural transformations do not necessarily coincide over space and time. However, data driven approaches typically collapse these into single indices or regression models, losing the nuances of individual components. This paper integrates housing market, demographic and social media data (SMD) to characterise different configurations of neighbourhood change in Leeds and Bradford, UK. Rates of change (2014-2019) were estimated over Lower Super Output Areas for house prices relative to the 250 nearest neighbouring areas, and for residential mobility, ethnic composition, unemployment and professional occupation. Approximately 1.6 million geo-tagged tweets, filtered for personal users using a large language model (LLM), were analysed using Structural Topic Models with socio-economic prevalence covariates, LLM based neighbourhood characterisation and text embeddings scored against gentrification and decline archetypes. These measures were used as inputs to a model-based cluster analysis, which identified six distinct neighbourhood types, and a spatially varying multinomial GAM was used to examine the effects of changes in the inputs on cluster membership. The results show repeated divergence between structural and discursive trajectories: rapid turnover that is invisible in local SMD discourse, heritage villages experiencing amenity and incomer pressure, a settled British-Pakistani community whose stability would be mis-characterised as stagnation or decline, and marginal areas accumulating strain with little on-line signal. This suggests that SMD derived measures can provide independent information on neighbourhood character rather than simply confirming structural indicators, although low SMD signals may reflect under-detection rather than an absence of change.

papers.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
papers.abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

papers.title: Gaussian Process Stochastic Frontiers with Two-Way Fixed Effects
papers.abstract: Parametric frontier restrictions and unobserved time heterogeneity can distort efficiency measurement in panel data. This paper develops a Bayesian stochastic frontier model with a Gaussian process prior and unrestricted individual and time effects that may be correlated with inputs. Conditional on inefficiency, orthogonal projection eliminates both sets of fixed effects, yielding a restricted likelihood that retains observation-specific inefficiency. Monte Carlo experiments show competitive performance under correct parametric specification and improved performance when benchmark models impose an incorrect frontier functional form or omit time effects. An application to Spanish dairy farms observed from 1999 to 2010 yields similar average technical efficiency across specifications, but a lower posterior mean of average returns to scale, with greater uncertainty, under the Gaussian process frontier. Models with year effects also yield more stable estimated efficiency profiles than the benchmark with a quadratic trend and time-input interactions. These findings show that conclusions about scale economies and efficiency dynamics depend on both frontier flexibility and the treatment of time heterogeneity.

papers.title: A new method of Ecological Inference based on the Cressie--Read power divergence
papers.abstract: Ecological inference aims to estimate the bivariate association structure between a pair of variables from the row and column totals of a set of contingency tables. The paper introduces a new approach based on minimizing the Cressie--Read power divergence, applied to the estimation of vote transitions between two elections. It also outlines a Fisher scoring algorithm and derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimator.

papers.title: Design-based causal inference for ROC curves
papers.abstract: In randomized experiments, causal inference traditionally focuses on the average treatment effect, yet comparing the treatment and control potential outcome distributions is often of interest. Under complete randomization, we adopt a design-based framework without imposing an outcome model to study the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which measures the proportion of treated outcomes exceeding each upper quantile of the control distribution. We propose an estimator that depends only on pooled outcome ranks, establish its asymptotic normality, and construct conservative variance estimators and confidence intervals. We also develop covariate adjustment directly for the ROC estimator, preserving the target estimand while achieving an asymptotic variance no larger than that of the unadjusted estimator. We further construct simultaneous confidence bands over an interior range of quantile levels and extend pointwise inference to the extreme upper tail of the control distribution, with both extensions accommodating covariate adjustment. Simulation studies and an application to a large-scale online learning experiment illustrate the proposed methods.

papers.title: Nonparametric predictive inference for interval-censored data: M-functions anchored to the self-consistent estimator
papers.abstract: Nonparametric predictive inference specifies the distribution of a future observation through M-functions, which are basic probability assignments on intervals. Here such a specification is proposed for data censored on the left, on the right or within intervals of arbitrary width. It is the union of two M-functions. The first rests on a post-data assumption under which each censored observation divides its predictive mass equally amongst the observations with regions inside its own, and it reproduces the right-censored theory exactly. The second combines the Turnbull estimator with one unconstrained unit of predictive mass. The resulting survival bounds contain the Turnbull estimator, lie inside the bounds from all completions of the data and need no enumeration. In simulated inspection schemes they were calibrated for fixed events and for the rank of a further observation, while the second member alone was not. Equal weights on all orderings allowed by the data give the first member whenever the regions are nested or disjoint. The method is compared with the Turnbull estimator on two interval-censored studies.

papers.title: Milk-removal feedback shapes lactation sustainability and daily output in a model of human lactation
papers.abstract: Milk production during lactation is dynamically regulated by milk removal, yet quantitative models linking feeding or pumping schedules to subsequent production remain scarce. We develop a minimal model describing milk accumulation and production between removal sessions, and the stimulation of subsequent production through milk removal. We compare different assumptions about how stimulation depends on the amount of milk removed or the duration of removal, and consider two removal protocols: prescribing either the removed amount or the removal duration. When stimulation depends on the removed amount, declining production can reduce subsequent stimulation and reinforce the decline. This leads to a critical wait interval beyond which no repeated constant schedule can sustain lactation. If stimulation is inefficient for small removal amounts but more efficient at intermediate amounts, the model can exhibit bistability: depending on the initial conditions, milk production either persists or ceases. In contrast, duration-dependent stimulation does not permit a zero-production state under continued removal, but can generate non-constant long-term dynamics under certain conditions. We further show that maximizing milk removal per session need not maximize daily output, because increased removal competes with session frequency. The framework provides a basis for testing alternative feedback hypotheses against longitudinal data and for optimizing feeding and pumping schedules.

papers.title: Will national renewable costs continue declining?
papers.abstract: Since the 1980s, the global average solar photovoltaic (PV) cost has decreased by about two orders of magnitude while the global average onshore wind cost has decreased by about one order of magnitude. But global averages are only part of the story: For both solar and wind, costs vary between countries by about an order of magnitude. We curate a comprehensive database of national costs and build predictive models for future costs by decomposing the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) into its components at the national level and modeling them separately. For solar we find that since 1990 the module cost and the balance of system (BOS) cost have both declined roughly exponentially at rates of 12% per year. In contrast, wind turbine cost has declined roughly exponentially by 4% per year, while BOS cost has not declined at all. This suggests that total global wind cost will approach a floor cost of about 35 USD/MWh, reaching about 43 USD/MWh in 2050, whereas global solar cost will continue to decline exponentially, reaching about 8 USD/MWh in 2050. For solar, about half of the cross-sectional variations in national LCOE costs is due to variations in capacity factors, though capital costs also play an important role. For wind, the cross-sectional variations are split approximately equally between capacity factor, capital costs, and investment costs. National BOS costs revert to global costs with a timescale of about 5-7 years, while variations in other factors are more persistent. We develop a simple model for predicting the deviations from global costs and show that it makes reasonable predictions with predictable errors. Finally, we compare our predictions to recent projections of integrated assessment models, and show that China has only accounted for about 0.05% of the overall decline in solar energy costs.

papers.title: The Illusion of an Automated German Census: Assessing the Feasibility of the 2031 Register-Based Census via Simulation
papers.abstract: The next German Census (2031) is planned to be the country's first fully register-based census, relying exclusively on administrative data sources. In addition to the population registers, ten further administrative registers are envisaged, covering a wide range of information, from driving licences to agricultural social insurance. This study simulates potential data-quality challenges in linking these registers using quasi-identifiers (QIDs), such as names and dates of birth. Using a synthetic population dataset (N=80,206,770), we systematically vary experimental factors related to register characteristics. Across the 1,458 experimental conditions studied, results vary considerably. Some plausible scenarios range from 500,000 to 1,000,000 false-negative linkage errors per linked register. These findings suggest that implementing an automated register-based census using the currently envisaged registers may prove challenging and could require substantial manual post-processing to achieve acceptable data quality.

papers.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
papers.abstract: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.

papers.title: Certifying a Sufficient Gaussian Dependence Regime for Learned Weighted FDR Control
papers.abstract: Learning hypothesis weights from informative auxiliary data can improve the power of multiple testing. Even when the weights are learned independently of the tests, the validity of weighted Benjamini-Hochberg depends on their joint distribution. We use reference observations to certify a sufficient dependence condition for one-sided Gaussian tests. An intersection-union test of uncertain correlation signs determines whether to apply weighted Benjamini-Hochberg or a prespecified fallback at an adjusted level. Under conditional separation of certification and testing, the procedure controls the false discovery rate (FDR) for every Gaussian correlation matrix satisfying the stated sampling assumptions and weight constraints. We establish a boundary obstruction to uniform certification and matching minimax sample-size bounds for worst-case pair sets and the all-pairs problem. In the parameter ranges of the matching bounds, the minimax sample size grows logarithmically with the number of checked pairs and quadratically with the inverse of their positive margin. For homogeneous Gaussian observations with known marginal variances, residual contrasts from the testing subjects provide an independent source of certification scores. Simulations with up to 4,950 checked pairs, comparisons under a common subject budget, and Gaussian designs based on correlations estimated from the Healthy Brain Network illustrate the trade-off between certification and detection power.

papers.title: Simple, general strategies for correcting the upward bias of calibration summaries of prediction models
papers.abstract: For clinical prediction models, calibration across the spectrum of predicted values is often assessed via flexible calibration curves and associated scalar summaries such as the integrated calibration index (ICI). However, these scalar summaries tend to have a finite-sample upward bias, as they are based on the absolute value of an estimate whose sampling distribution can cross zero. We show the mechanism underlying this bias and quantify its magnitude as a function of the true calibration error and its variance. This mechanism motivates easily implementable methods for reducing the bias (plug-in and inversion methods, each applied locally or globally) that are applicable to any smoothing method that generates an estimate and its sampling variance for each point on the calibration curve. These methods are general in that 1) they can be used for different outcome types (continuous, binary, time-to-event, as well as counterfactual outcomes for models that predict treatment benefit), and 2) the resulting bias-adjusted calibration error curves yield bias-corrected estimates of other metrics such as quantile-based ones (e.g., E50 and E90). Focusing on ICI as an exemplary metric, numerical and case studies demonstrate that the upward bias can be substantial, especially when the sample is small and the true ICI is close to zero. Results show that the Global Inversion method removed the most bias, particularly when the bias was substantial, although it could slightly increase the mean absolute error if the bias was small.

papers.title: Fairness-Regularized Principal Component Analysis
papers.abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) optimizes aggregate reconstruction accuracy but may represent heterogeneous groups unevenly. We study fairness-regularized PCA, which balances aggregate reconstruction risk against worst-group reconstruction regret, and establish its population and statistical properties. First, we characterize the reconstruction-fairness trade-off and show that, under a nondegeneracy condition, a small fairness penalty reduces worst-group regret to first order while increasing aggregate reconstruction risk only to second order. This reveals a vanishing initial marginal cost of improving fairness. We also identify conditions under which the regularization path remains locally constant. A minimax spectral characterization shows that, under an optimal effective eigengap condition, the convex relaxation is exact and Fair PCA is equivalent to ordinary PCA with endogenously adjusted group weights. Second, we develop a statistical theory for estimating fairness-regularized principal subspaces. A uniform eigengap over the set of possibly nonunique dual optimizers implies polyhedral identification and quadratic growth, yielding first-order perturbation bounds and convergence rates that accommodate growing dimensions, ranks, and numbers of groups. Third, we establish uniform recovery of the reconstruction-fairness path and theoretical guarantees for data-adaptive penalty selection. Simulations and an NHANES accelerometry application demonstrate substantial improvements in worst-group representation quality with minimal loss of aggregate reconstruction accuracy.

papers.title: Shooting for Fit: Risk-Averse Stochastic Roster Construction from Bayesian Shot-Pattern Models
papers.abstract: Roster construction is a critical decision problem in professional basketball, requiring teams to balance player quality, player complementarity, and financial constraints under uncertainty. Existing roster optimization models primarily rely on individual player ratings and aggregate performance statistics, which provide limited information about how players' offensive contributions vary with their teammates. Recent advances in player-tracking technology have enabled statistical analyses of spatial shooting patterns, but these insights have rarely informed roster construction. We bridge this gap by developing a data-driven, risk-averse two-stage stochastic optimization framework for NBA roster construction. We first develop a Bayesian modeling framework that combines player statistics and spatial shot-chart data to identify player roles and estimate how teammate composition influences shot selection, shooting frequency, and scoring efficiency. The resulting model provides uncertainty-quantified offensive values for hypothetical five-player lineups, including combinations that have never played together. We then formulate roster construction as a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program that optimizes player acquisitions under NBA salary-cap regulations while allowing lineup playing-time allocations to adapt to uncertain player roles. We evaluate the framework using 240 team-offseason decisions over eight seasons and two additional held-out seasons. The results demonstrate that incorporating spatial shooting compatibility substantially changes optimal roster decisions and improves predicted offensive performance relative to approaches based on individual player values. We further find that flexibility in allocating playing time across lineups absorbs much of the uncertainty about player roles.

papers.title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.

papers.title: Learning to Infer: Statistical Inference through Meta Learning
papers.abstract: We study meta learning for statistical inference, in which neural networks learn inference rules from simulated tasks and apply them to new datasets without parameter updates, providing a form of in-context learning. We draw on statistical decision theory to design training objectives whose population minimizers are Bayes rules and exploit their connections to classical inference procedures to establish frequentist guarantees for the learned rules. The structure of classical inference procedures also motivates the design of our neural network architecture, called Residual Recurrent Deep Sets (RRDS), which repeatedly aggregates information across observations in a permutation-invariant manner and refines its internal state through residual updates. Under suitable regularity and training conditions, we establish asymptotic efficiency in parameter estimation, consistency in model selection, and variable selection guarantees in high-dimensional regression models. The RRDS architecture allows us to avoid the curse of sample size that arises in generic neural network approximation when the network takes the entire dataset as input. For fixed-dimensional models, the network size and the number of meta training tasks need only grow polynomially in the sample size; under additional analyticity conditions, these requirements improve to polylogarithmic growth in network size and nearly linear growth in the number of training tasks. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample advantages of the learned inference rules over classical methods.

papers.title: Exclusion and internal structure in the association/dissociation kinetics of DNA-binding proteins in the fast diffusion limit
papers.abstract: In many canonical biophysical and biochemical contexts, complex diffusing DNA-binding proteins undergoing nonspecific adsorption and desorption can exist in different conformational states. Equilibrium binding theories and kinetic models of competing ligands provide a basis for describing these systems. Coupling the internal conformational kinetics of bound proteins to exclusion and diffusion requires tracking both protein positions and binding states. Closed-form, tractable mathematical models that accurately describe the stochastic dynamics of structured proteins that bind to and diffuse along DNA are lacking. Here, we develop a new coarse-grained stochastic model of nonspecific DNA-protein binding in the fast diffusion regime, from which we derive an effective Markov model and its corresponding mean-field approximation that incorporates protein footprint size and conformational switching. We fit our new model quantitatively to previously measured dynamics of Replication Protein A (RPA) binding to ssDNA. Finally, by including multisegment binding states, our analysis captures facilitated exchange, revealing how multisegment architecture balances high affinity with rapid remodeling. Our theoretical model applies broadly to many other DNA-binding protein systems, including nucleosomes, ssDNA-binding proteins, and other multisegment complexes, providing accurate predictions and new strategies for evaluating experimental data.

papers.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
papers.abstract: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.

papers.title: Bayesian Latent Functional Mediation Analysis with Application to Population-Scale Single-Cell Data
papers.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing studies pair cell-level gene expression with donor-level genotypes, enabling investigation of genetic regulation across cellular states. Mediation analysis in this setting must account for cells nested within donors and for unobserved cellular states. We propose a Bayesian latent functional mediation model that decomposes the association between genotype and distal gene expression into a component mediated through a candidate cis gene and a remaining direct component. The model represents expression as donor-specific trajectories over a shared latent state coordinate constrained by coarse cell annotations. Joint inference propagates uncertainty in latent states, trajectories, and mediation parameters into state-specific effect functions and their integrated summaries. Simulations show that effect recovery improves with the number of donors and that averaging expression within donors can change the mediated and direct components even when the total association is preserved. In 403,087 CD4+ T cells from 961 OneK1K donors, higher rs1131017 G-allele dosage was associated with higher RPS26 expression across the fitted state domain. The estimated RPS26-mediated component of the association with BAX expression was negative over most of the domain and was partly offset by a positive direct component, yielding a smaller negative integrated total association. In sensitivity analyses conditional on estimated donor trajectories, all three integrated effects retained their signs, with 95% credible intervals excluding zero, at the five examined coefficient-level residual correlations with $|ρ_s|\leq 0.3$. The mediated and direct effects reversed signs at $ρ_s=-0.5$, while the integrated total association remained negative across all seven tested settings.

papers.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
papers.abstract: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.

papers.title: Cutting Bus Service Without Cutting Access: Persistent Homology of Service Deserts and Timetable Reductions
papers.abstract: Japanese bus operators are withdrawing service for lack of drivers, and the choice of which trips to withdraw determines who keeps a bus. We measure service at each stop from vehicle GPS and smart-card records, without timetables, and use persistent homology of walking and walking-plus-waiting time to find enclosed service deserts: pockets surrounded by service but beyond walking distance from it. Around Tsukuba, 35 such pockets lie more than 800m from any station or hourly stop. The 17 that are fully ringed by walkable service hold 18,446 residents. We compare two 2020 timetable reductions by Kanto Railway with random reductions and a heuristic frontier of same-size, capacity-feasible alternatives. At two and four buses an hour, both reductions protected service better than random reductions. No alternative found by the sweep dominates the state-of-emergency timetable. The summer timetable is dominated: it withdrew hourly service from 5,253 residents around stops with almost no morning riders, whereas same-size alternatives kept it for all of them at equal waiting. Averages hide a tail: under the actual timetables, 5.9% and 3.9% of residents are at stops whose expected wait rises by 10 minutes or more, against 0.5% and 0.3% in the alternatives, and capping the increase at 10 minutes at every served stop is feasible at the operator's sizes. If half the removed hours become paid hours saved, the labor saving of both reductions and their main alternatives fall short of the fare revenue on the removed trips.

papers.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
papers.abstract: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

papers.title: How Many Sources, Not Just How Many Problems: Planning the Precision of LLM Evaluations from Earlier Results
papers.abstract: When benchmark problems share sources, such as variants of one template or tasks from one repository, an evaluation budget must fix the number of sources as well as the number of problems. We ask whether pilot data or earlier evaluation results can predict, before an evaluation is run, how much the standard deviation (SD) of the score grows when the same budget is concentrated on fewer sources. We use the classical design effect with an intraclass correlation estimated on data disjoint from those used to check the prediction. On GSM-Symbolic, 100 problems drawn as 10 templates x 10 variants have an SD of 9.2 pp against 2.7 pp from 100 templates; pilot data on 15 other questions predict the ratio as 3.49 against 3.52 measured on held-out questions (medians over 20 splits; single splits err by -13% to +16%), once the actual sampling plan is included. On SWE-bench Verified, 10 randomly selected public submissions predict the median ratio for 119 other submissions within 3% for 2 or more repositories, and 3 submissions are nearly as good. Dropping the finite-population terms from the design prediction gives errors of 13-21% on GSM-Symbolic, where it reduces to the textbook formula, and 25-35% on SWE-bench. Widening iid intervals by the square root of the pilot design effect brings pass@1 coverage on concentrated designs to 0.93-0.98, but not pass@16 (0.85, 0.76). We also report two lessons for anyone validating such predictions: split pilot and held-out data by question source, not by difficulty version, and do not read a good fit of the formula as evidence of source clustering (MATH-500). The method is not new; we contribute a held-out test of its advance predictions and a recipe for using them. Code: https://github.com/Guang627/deff-eval

papers.title: New fast and accurate estimators of the five-parameter lambda distribution (FPLD) with practical applications
papers.abstract: When fitting parametric densities, simple distributions are often chosen because they are computationally efficient to estimate and easy to interpret. However, simplicity can result in important features of the data being missed. This paper introduces fast and reliable estimators of the five-parameter lambda distribution (FPLD). The FPLD is highly flexible, can take many different shapes, and provides greater control over skewness and tail behaviour than distributions with fewer parameters. Simulations are provided to demonstrate the excellent performance of the proposed estimators compared with existing methods, at a fraction of the computational cost. Applications in which speed and accuracy are important are also provided, with comparisons to commonly used but potentially overly simplistic approaches. Finally, an R package implementing the proposed estimators and a web application that allows users to determine the FPLD parameters required to approximate well-known distributions are provided.

papers.title: A Robust Approach for Regression Analysis of Panel Count Data with Time-varying Covariates
papers.abstract: The validity of statistical inference for panel count data with time-varying covariates depends on the correct specification of within-subject correlation structures; misspecification often leads to questionable inference. To alleviate, robust inference has been proposed for mean models, which implicitly assume monotone mean functions. When covariate values fluctuate with time, however, the assumed monotonicity becomes unrealistic. In this research, we propose a robust inference based on rate models that are free of such constraints. Since the asymptotic variance has no closed form under the rate model, we further develop computationally efficient robust variance estimators using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, thus sidestepping the need for computationally intensive numerical methods, which could undermine the robustness. Rigorous theoretical development is provided in support of parameter estimation and inference. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method. We present a real clinical application to illustrate the use of the proposed method.

papers.title: Refinements to precision-information imputation in meta-analysis of survival rates: Boundary correction and cross-study borrowing
papers.abstract: Meta-analyses of survival rates require precision information, such as standard errors (SEs), which is often unreported. We previously proposed imputing missing SEs from reported survival rates, sample sizes, and risk-set sizes. The original method has two limitations. First, it replaces Kaplan--Meier estimates of 1 with 0.99 regardless of sample size. Second, when the risk-set size is unavailable, it uses the total event count as a fallback. The count is often unreported, and the fallback can also substantially overestimate SEs. We propose a sample-size-dependent boundary correction based on a pseudo-event and a method that borrows time-specific event information from studies with available risk-set sizes. In simulations, the boundary correction was more stable than fixed replacement, and borrowing reduced study-level SE imputation bias. Borrowing generally improved precision by retaining studies with missing SEs that lacked both risk-set sizes and event counts.

papers.title: k-Nearest Neighbors estimation of the drift of an ergodic diffusion process under Osgood regularity
papers.abstract: The k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) algorithm is a widely used machine learning method with well-established theoretical guarantees for consistent estimation in multivariate settings and functional time series analysis. In the context of nonparametric estimation of the coefficients of ergodic diffusion processes, however, its use has so far been mainly illustrated through numerical experiments. The main contribution of this paper is to establish theoretical consistency results for drift kNN estimators over both compact and non-compact intervals, under relatively weak regularity conditions on the coefficients of the underlying ergodic diffusion process. The theoretical results are completed with numerical illustrations.

papers.title: Sharp sensitivity bounds and maximin policy learning under violations of principal ignorability
papers.abstract: Identification of assignment effects among compliers often relies on the untestable assumption of principal ignorability. Sensitivity analyses based only on outcome means and ranges can admit complier distributions incompatible with the observed data. We develop a distributional sensitivity model preserving the full observed outcome distributions and identified complier proportions. The challenge is to recover latent complier distributions within observed mixtures while ensuring compatibility across assignment arms. We characterize exactly which pairs arise from a single compatible full-data law, obtaining sharp bounds on effects and policy values. This characterization shows how complier proportions constrain departures from principal ignorability and why informative bounds remain without a finite sensitivity restriction. Accounting for principal scores in both population weights and sensitivity limits, we establish conditions for doubly robust consistency, semiparametric efficiency, and conservative bounds under quantile misspecification. Double robustness requires consistent principal score estimation. We also develop maximin decision-tree policies with value consistency and inference guarantees. Numerical studies demonstrate gains from retaining distributional information, and an Oregon Health Insurance Experiment application examines implications for complier effects and assignment policies.

papers.title: Unsupervised and explainable authorization of change point in multivariate industrial data for trustworthy system and process monitoring
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a Change point Hypothesis Assessment for Significance in Multivariate data (CHASM) - a novel non-parametric approach for evaluating the significance of change points detected in multivariate data, especially relevant for a trustworthy autonomous industrial system. The method is highly scalable, doesn't require data labeling, and allows for customizable evaluation criteria, such as inter-component relationships. Its non-parametric nature broadens applicability to non-Gaussian distributed data. CHASM incorporates robust auxiliary statistics that maintain reliability even in the presence of outliers, enabling accurate assessment of change point significance for complex data. Beyond statistical significance testing, CHASM also facilitates root-cause analysis of detected changes. It offers a solution expected by practitioners for validating change points identified by segmentation-based algorithms, particularly those lacking rigorous statistical foundations. To support situation aware decision making, a {trustworthy factor} is introduced and its performance demonstrated for simulated and real-world data recorded in machine monitoring system. Using MAPE, it was evidenced that the two-stage procedure - identification of the change point and authorization of the change point - significantly outperforms (23-fold in the reported experiment) the one-stage scheme. All these are essential in real-world applications, where overfitting and false alarms can lead to loss of trust in technical solutions.

papers.title: An iterative procedure for statistical calibration
papers.abstract: We study the iterative proportional fitting procedure (IPFP) under multiple pushforward constraints, motivated by model calibration. The goal is to find a distribution on model parameters whose pushforward by models matches data distributions. The classic convergence result of IPFP under marginal constraints establish convergence of IPFP under suitable regularity conditions and develop a variant of sequential importance sampling to approximate the iterative procedure. We also propose a related procedure for constructing a high probability parameter region. Simulation studies illustrate the performance of these methods. Finally, we apply IPFP to COVID19 ensemble forecasting. Variation of Covid strains across regions can lead to variation in surge rates and thus affect forecasting accuracy. To capture the variation, we estimate a probability distribution of epidemiological model parameters using early stage surge data from an ensemble of regions. We then propagate the distribution through the model to forecast both the ensemble's overall trend and its variability.
